title: Reciprocity of a similitude pair under a perfect pairing
statement:
Let $K$ be a field, let $V$ and $W$ be finite-dimensional $K$-vector spaces [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace] with dimensions [def-weil-vector-space-dimension] $\dim_KV$, $\dim_KW$, and let $\beta:V\times W\to K$ be a $K$-bilinear map that is perfect, meaning that the two induced $K$-linear maps $V\to\operatorname{Hom}_K(W,K)$, $v\mapsto\beta(v,-)$, and $W\to\operatorname{Hom}_K(V,K)$, $w\mapsto\beta(-,w)$, are bijective. Let $F:V\to V$ and $G:W\to W$ be $K$-linear endomorphisms and $c\in K^\times$ a nonzero scalar such that

$$
\beta(Fv,Gw)=c\,\beta(v,w)\qquad(v\in V,\ w\in W)
$$

(a *similitude pair* with multiplier $c$). Fix an indeterminate $T$, write $P_F(T)=\det(1-TF\mid V)\in K[T]$ and $P_G(T)=\det(1-TG\mid W)\in K[T]$ for the reverse characteristic polynomials [def-weil-reverse-characteristic-polynomial], $\chi_F(T)=\det(T-F\mid V)\in K[T]$ for the characteristic polynomial [def-weil-characteristic-polynomial], and $\det(F\mid V),\det(G\mid W)\in K$ for the determinants [def-weil-endomorphism-determinant]. Put $n=\dim_KV$. Then:

1. $\dim_KW=\dim_KV=n$.

2. $F$ and $G$ are invertible, and $\det(F\mid V)\cdot\det(G\mid W)=c^{\,n}$.

3. $\deg P_F=\deg P_G=n$, and $P_F(0)=P_G(0)=1$; more precisely, after transporting $G$ along the isomorphism $W\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Hom}_K(V,K)$, $w\mapsto\beta(-,w)$, it becomes $c\,(F^{-1})^\vee$ (the scalar $c$ times the transpose of the inverse of $F$), and consequently

$$
\det(F\mid V)\cdot P_G(T)=(-1)^{n}\,\chi_F(cT)\qquad\text{in }K[T].
$$

4. For every ring homomorphism $\iota:K\to L$ into an algebraically closed field $L$ [def-weil-algebraic-closure], the multiset of reciprocal roots of $P_G$ in $L$ [lem-weil-reciprocal-root-factorization] is the image of the multiset of reciprocal roots of $P_F$ in $L$ under $\alpha\mapsto\iota(c)/\alpha$, with multiplicities [def-weil-root-multiplicity]: if $(P_F)_L(T)=\prod_{r=1}^{n}(1-\alpha_rT)$ in $L[T]$, then $(P_G)_L(T)=\prod_{r=1}^{n}\bigl(1-\iota(c)\alpha_r^{-1}T\bigr)$. Equivalently, the roots of $(P_G)_L$ in $L$, counted with multiplicity, are the $(\iota(c)z)^{-1}$ for the roots $z$ of $(P_F)_L$. In particular (with $\iota$ the identity when $K$ is algebraically closed) the eigenvalues of $G$ in $L$, counted with algebraic multiplicity, are the $\iota(c)/\alpha$ for the eigenvalues $\alpha$ of $F$ in $L$.

proof.text: Choose a basis $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ of $V$, as in [def-weil-vector-space-dimension]. Such a basis exists from finite generation: process a finite spanning list, retaining a vector precisely when it is not in the span of the retained predecessors. The retained list is independent by looking at the last nonzero coefficient of a proposed relation, and spans the original list by induction. Let $v_i^*$ send $\sum_j x_jv_j$ to $x_i$; uniqueness of coordinates shows that these are linear and that every linear functional $\lambda$ equals $\sum_i\lambda(v_i)v_i^*$.

source.place: Step 1: perfect-pairing identification, coordinates on the first space.

proof.text: Let $J:W\to V^*$ be $J(w)(v)=\beta(v,w)$. It is a bijective linear map by hypothesis. Define $w_j=J^{-1}(v_j^*)$, so $\beta(v_i,w_j)=\delta_{ij}$. Applying $J$ to a relation among the $w_j$ shows independence by evaluation at each $v_i$. For any $w$, the functional $J(w)$ equals $\sum_j\beta(v_j,w)v_j^*$, so injectivity of $J$ gives $w=\sum_j\beta(v_j,w)w_j$. Thus the $w_j$ form a basis, and [def-weil-vector-space-dimension] gives $\dim_KW=n$. These arguments include $n=0$, when injectivity of $J:W\to0$ forces $W=0$.

source.place: Step 1: the pairing identifies the second space with the dual; equal cardinalities.

proof.text: We record explicitly the short determinant manipulations used below, all from the Leibniz formula [def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant]. For any $m\times m$ matrix $M$ over any commutative ring $R$, $\det I_m=1$: only the identity permutation contributes, also for $m=0$. Scaling every entry by $s\in R$ multiplies each summand by $s^m$, so $\det(sM)=s^m\det M$. For transpose, the summand $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_k M_{k,\sigma(k)}$ becomes $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma^{-1})\prod_j M_{\sigma^{-1}(j),j}$ by $j=\sigma(k)$; reindexing the permutation sum by inversion gives $\det M^t=\det M$. Finally a ring homomorphism applied to the finite signed sum and its products gives the determinant of the entrywise image matrix. No invertibility or nonempty index set is needed in these formulas.

source.place: Steps 1–2: elementary determinant calculations expanded from the permutation formula.

proof.text: Let $A$ and $B$ be the matrices of $F$ and $G$ in the two bases above. Bilinearity gives $(A^tB)_{ij}=\sum_k A_{ki}B_{kj}=\beta(Fv_i,Gw_j)=c\delta_{ij}$, hence $A^tB=cI_n$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-cauchy-binet] with both sizes equal to $n$: the sole $n$-element subset of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ is the whole set, so $\det(A^tB)=\det(A^t)\det B$. Step 3 therefore gives $\det A\det B=c^n$. By [def-weil-endomorphism-determinant] these are the two endomorphism determinants. Since $c\ne0$, their product is nonzero, so both determinants are nonzero.

source.place: Step 2: determinant product from the similitude relation, before eigenvalues.

proof.text: By the invertibility criterion stated in [def-weil-endomorphism-determinant], both $F$ and $G$ are invertible. To identify the transported operator without assuming any spectral decomposition, take $\lambda=J(w)$ and $v\in V$. The similitude condition at $(F^{-1}v,w)$ gives $J(Gw)(v)=\beta(v,Gw)=c\beta(F^{-1}v,w)=c\lambda(F^{-1}v)$. Hence $JGJ^{-1}=c(F^{-1})^\vee$, for the specified map $J$, proving the transport clause as well as invertibility.

source.place: Step 1: explicit formula for the transported endomorphism on the dual.

proof.text: For any $n\times n$ matrix $M$, expand $\det(I_n-TM)$ by [def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant]. Each summand is a product of $n$ polynomials of degree at most one, so the degree is at most $n$. Its constant term is $\det I_n=1$ by step 3. The coefficient of $T^n$ comes by taking $-T M_{\sigma(k),k}$ from every factor; summing gives $(-1)^n\det M$. For $M=A$ and $M=B$ this coefficient is nonzero by step 4; thus [def-weil-reverse-characteristic-polynomial] gives $\deg P_F=\deg P_G=n$ and $P_F(0)=P_G(0)=1$. For $n=0$ these computations give the constant polynomial $1$ of degree zero.

source.place: Steps 1–2: degrees, constant coefficients and leading determinants in the Frobenius factors.

proof.text:
Regard the matrices as matrices over $K[T]$ by the constant-coefficient inclusion. From $A^tB=cI_n$ we have $A^t(I_n-TB)=A^t-cTI_n$. Apply the square case of [lem-weil-pbc-cauchy-binet] over this commutative ring and use step 3 (transpose, scalar $-1$, and coefficient inclusion) to obtain
$$\det A\,P_G(T)=\det(A^t-cTI_n)=(-1)^n\det(cTI_n-A^t)=(-1)^n\det(cTI_n-A)=(-1)^n\chi_F(cT).$$
Here transposition fixes $cTI_n$, $P_G(T)=\det(I_n-TB)$ by the matrix description in [def-weil-reverse-characteristic-polynomial], and $\chi_F(U)=\det(UI_n-A)$ by the matrix description in [def-weil-characteristic-polynomial]; the substitution $U\mapsto cT$ is a ring homomorphism $K[U]\to K[T]$, so by step 3 it carries $\det(UI_n-A)$ to $\det(cTI_n-A)$. This proves the polynomial identity with its sign, without division by a polynomial.

source.place: Steps 1–3: determinant identity giving reciprocal characteristic polynomials.

proof.text:
Fix a ring homomorphism $\iota:K	o L$ to an algebraically closed field. It is injective: if $x
e0$ and $\iota(x)=0$, then $1=\iota(xx^{-1})=0$, impossible. By [lem-weil-coefficientwise-extension-degree], $P=(P_F)_L$ and $Q=(P_G)_L$ have degree $n$ and constant term $1$. Applying the coefficientwise ring homomorphism to step 7 gives, with $a=\iota(\det F)
e0$ and $b=\iota(c)
e0$,
$$aQ(T)=(-1)^n(\chi_F)_L(bT).$$
That substitution commutes with coefficient extension follows by writing $\chi_F(U)=\sum_k h_kU^k$: both sides have coefficients $\iota(h_k)\,\iota(c)^k$.

source.place: Step 1: eigenvalue comparison after a field embedding; explicit coefficient extension.

proof.text: By [lem-weil-reciprocal-root-factorization] applied to $P_F$, choose $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n\in L^\times$ with $P(T)=\prod_{r=1}^n(1-\alpha_rT)$. Its clause 3 identifies this family, with repetitions, with the reciprocal-root multiset. It suffices to calculate for this family: that same clause shows that any other factorization of the indicated length is a reordering, so the product formula below applies to every family occurring in the statement.

source.place: Step 1: reciprocal roots, with algebraic multiplicities, in place of an assumed eigenbasis.

proof.text:
The identity $P_F(T)=T^n\chi_F(1/T)$ of [lem-weil-reverse-charpoly-eq-reverse], mapped by $\iota$ and then by the ring homomorphism $T\mapsto U^{-1}$ into $L[U,U^{-1}]$ and multiplied by $U^n$, gives, in $L[U,U^{-1}]$,
$$(\chi_F)_L(U)=U^nP(U^{-1})=\prod_{r=1}^n(U-\alpha_r).$$
Both sides are polynomials, so this is a polynomial equality: the inclusion into Laurent polynomials preserves every coefficient and is injective. Comparing the coefficients of $T^n$ in step 9 and step 6 after $\iota$ gives $(-1)^n\prod_r\alpha_r=(-1)^n a$, hence $\prod_r\alpha_r=a$. Thus step 8 becomes
$$aQ(T)=(-1)^n\prod_r(bT-\alpha_r)=\Bigl(\prod_r\alpha_r\Bigr)\prod_r(1-b\alpha_r^{-1}T)=a\prod_r(1-b\alpha_r^{-1}T).$$
Cancellation of the nonzero scalar $a$ in $L[T]$ proves precisely the asserted factorization of $(P_G)_L$.

source.place: Steps 1–2: reciprocal eigenvalues and determinant product via the actual factorizations.

proof.text: Each $b\alpha_r^{-1}$ is nonzero. Apply clause 3 of [lem-weil-reciprocal-root-factorization] to $P_G$: step 10 identifies its reciprocal roots, with exactly their multiplicities, as $b/\alpha_r$. Its ordinary roots are therefore $\alpha_r/b$. The ordinary roots of $P_F$ are $z_r=\alpha_r^{-1}$, so $\alpha_r/b=(bz_r)^{-1}$, including repetitions. Finally the identity of [lem-weil-reverse-charpoly-eq-reverse] for $G$ gives $(\chi_G)_L(U)=\prod_r(U-b/\alpha_r)$ just as in step 10. Since eigenvalues counted with algebraic multiplicity mean roots of the characteristic polynomial with root multiplicities [def-weil-root-multiplicity], the eigenvalue assertion follows from these two characteristic-polynomial factorizations. Empty products give all the asserted identities when $n=0$.

source.place: Step 1: eigenvalue multiset and step 2: determinants, retaining multiplicities.
